stories.title: AI Rewrites the Chip That Runs AI
stories.story:
For decades, semiconductor design has followed a fixed rhythm: human engineers write register-transfer-level code — the precise logic describing how a chip's circuits behave — spend years tuning it, then hand the result to fabrication. The assumption baked into that rhythm is that squeezing more performance out of already-optimized silicon requires human intuition and accumulated institutional knowledge. OpenAI just cracked that assumption open.

In a technical report published November 18, OpenAI disclosed that its models rewrote AMD's flagship GPU circuits in SystemVerilog RTL and found up to 14% improvement in the composite measure engineers call PPA — power consumption, performance, and silicon area. The baseline wasn't raw code; it was circuitry AMD engineers had already spent years optimizing. AMD verified the results, folded some of the AI-proposed changes into a design it sent for manufacturing, and confirmed single-digit PPA gains on key blocks of its next-generation flagship CPU too. What ordinarily takes roughly a year of tuning was done in under five months.

The verification step matters as much as the numbers. Each rewrite had to pass through Synopsys EDA tools, which confirm that a modified circuit still behaves identically to the original before any PPA measurement is even taken. OpenAI is now codifying this workflow into a product with Synopsys, training a dedicated model — GPT-Synopsys — to operate chip-design tools autonomously.

The recursive implication is the story's real twist: AI is now improving the hardware that AI runs on. If the feedback loop holds — better chips enabling better models, better models compressing chip design cycles further — the semiconductor industry's traditional five-year design cadence may no longer be the binding constraint on AI progress. The bottleneck shifts from silicon to whoever controls the design models.
stories.hook: The chip that runs the AI was designed, in part, by the AI.
stories.source: OpenAI technical report, November 18, 2026; reporting via Forbes, unite.ai, hwbusters.com

stories.title: Databricks Hits $225 Billion While Public AI Markets Crack
stories.story:
Here is the split screen that defines the AI economy right now: the Nasdaq 100 just shed 10.4 percent in a single week, with public AI companies hammered by fears of circular financing and vanishing margins. Meanwhile, Databricks — a company that most consumers have never heard of — is in talks to raise several billion dollars at a $225 billion valuation, up from $190 billion just ninety-nine days ago in August.

The number matters not for its size but for what it reveals about structure. Databricks is not a model company. It does not make the AI that people talk to. It makes the plumbing: the data lakehouse that lets enterprises store, clean, and pipe their data into AI applications. Its closest public rival, Snowflake, now trades at roughly $90 billion — less than half the Databricks ask — which means either private investors are delusional or public markets are punishing anything that smells like AI without fully pricing the unglamorous infrastructure layer underneath it.

The business fundamentals lend some cover to the bulls. Databricks disclosed a revenue run-rate above $7 billion growing at more than 80 percent year over year, with positive free cash flow — a combination that is genuinely rare at this scale. At $225 billion that works out to roughly 32 times run-rate revenue: aggressive, but not science fiction for a category that may have no ceiling.

What this implies is a bifurcation that will not resolve quietly. If the Databricks round closes at the reported terms, it validates the thesis that the real money in AI accrues to whoever owns the data layer, not the model layer. If it stalls, it signals that private AI prices are finally gravitating toward public ones — and the reckoning begins.
stories.hook: The picks-and-shovels theory of AI gold rushes: the company supplying the pipes just got valued at more than twice its public-market rival.

stories.title: Oracle Burns Its Last Bullet to Build the AI Cloud
stories.story:
Three weeks ago, Oracle did something unusual even by the standards of this AI spending frenzy: it raised $20 billion in a single day. Half came from equity — 86 million new shares priced at $116 each, an 11.2% discount to the prior close. The other half came from senior notes carrying coupon rates between 7% and 8.65%, the kind of borrowing costs that signal urgency rather than opportunism. Shares fell roughly 7% on the day of announcement.

What makes the move structurally interesting is what Oracle said at its Investor Day just five days earlier: it would raise no more than $20 billion in new external capital through fiscal 2030, excluding refinancing. By executing the full raise in one transaction, Oracle used its entire self-imposed ceiling in a single afternoon. There is no more runway under that framework. Whatever Oracle builds with this money, it must work.

The destination is AI infrastructure — data centers, compute capacity, and the cloud database business that Oracle has been quietly winning as enterprises find that running inference at scale is a database problem as much as a GPU problem. Oracle's stated target is $225 billion in annual revenue by FY2030, roughly four times what it earns today. The $20 billion is seed capital for that ambition, not a hedge.

The timing, against a week when the Nasdaq 100 fell over 10% and the AI circular-financing bear case was airing on CNBC, is a kind of corporate bet-hedging in reverse: public markets are losing faith precisely as Oracle commits the most capital it ever will. If the AI infrastructure buildout proves real, Oracle positioned itself cheaply. If it proves circular, Oracle just levered up at the worst moment.
stories.hook: Oracle just spent its last bullet — the question is whether it picked the right target.
stories.source: Oracle SEC filings (Form 8-K, Form 424B5, Nov. 2–4, 2026); FinanceFeeds; GuruFocus
